1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. JSON: JavaScript Object Notation; API: application programming interface

  • Tool use and function calling: the round trip from definition to result
  • Writing tool descriptions and schemas
  • Error handling in tools
  • Patterns: harness dispatch, client-side versus server-side tools, approval patterns
  • Tool set construction best practices

2The Tool Round Trip

Running case

Tidewater Connects the Policy System

  • The assistant must look up policies, check claim status and open a payment request
  • These actions live in Tidewater's internal systems: Claude cannot reach them on its own

Step What happens
Define Each tool has a name, a description and an input_schema (JSON Schema)
Call Claude decides to use a tool and returns a tool_use block (name, id, input); stop_reason is "tool_use"
Run Your harness validates the input and runs the function (this is the dispatch: map tool name to code)
Return Send a tool_result (matching tool_use_id) in the next user message
Continue Claude reads the result and answers or calls another tool; stop on end_turn 
{
  "name": "get_policy",
  "description": "Returns coverage limits, deductible and status for ONE policy. Input: a policy number like TW-204518. Use for policy questions; use lookup_claim for claim status.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": { "policy_number": { "type": "string", "pattern": "^TW-[0-9]{6}$" } },
    "required": ["policy_number"]
  }
}
  • Claude can request several tools at once (parallel tool calls); return all results together. tool_choice controls whether a tool must be called (auto, any, a named tool, none).
  • Descriptions drive selection: say what the tool does, its inputs, when to use it and when not to; precise schemas (patterns, enums) prevent bad input.

[Verify live] Forced tool use (tool_choice of any or a named tool) is not supported on some current models; see the define-tools page for alternatives such as strict tool use. As of 8 November 2026.

Exam tip

The model's tool arguments are untrusted input: validate them in your harness before running anything.

3Client-Side Versus Server-Side Tools

Client tools Server tools
Runs In your application On Anthropic's infrastructure
Examples Your internal APIs; bash and text_editor (Anthropic-defined schemas, your execution) web_search, web_fetch, code_execution, tool_search
Flow tool_use → you run it → tool_result You see results directly; no execution on your side
Control Full: validation, permissions, logging Less: configure and trust the platform
Use for Internal systems, private data, side effects General capabilities that need no access to your systems
Exam tip

Internal systems and private data call for client tools; server tools suit general capabilities such as web search.

4Error Handling, Dispatch and Approval

  • Return errors to the model in the tool_result with is_error: true and a clear message (what failed, whether to retry, what to try instead). An exception that crashes the harness gives the model nothing to recover from.
  • Validate input before running (types, ranges, authorization of the caller, not just the model's request). The model's arguments are untrusted input.
  • Timeouts and idempotency: bound tool runtime; give side-effecting tools an idempotency key so retries are safe.
  • Prune results: return only the fields needed (Module 9).

Approval patterns

Pattern When
Auto-approve Read-only, low-risk tools
Human confirmation Sensitive or irreversible actions (payments, deletions, emails)
Policy/permission rules and hooks Deterministic allow, deny or ask by tool and arguments
Dry run then commit Show what would change; apply after approval

5Building a Good Tool Set

Practice Why
Few, distinct tools Too many or overlapping tools degrade selection
Clear names and boundary-stating descriptions The description is the main selection signal
One purpose per tool with a precise schema Reliable use and testing
Consistent naming and error format Predictable behavior
Return concise, relevant results Saves context
Least privilege A tool exposes only what it needs; separate read and write tools
Test tool selection with ambiguous requests Catches misrouting early
Exam tip

Wrong tool chosen or misused → improve the description and schema first; sensitive action → approval gate plus validation in code, not a prompt sentence.

6Exam Q&A

S1Claude must call Tidewater's internal claims API. Where does the API call actually run?

  • AOn Anthropic's servers automatically, as part of the model response
  • BInside the model, which executes the code by itself
  • CIn the user's browser only
  • DIn the developer's harness: the app runs the function after a tool_use request
Show the answer

Answer: D. For client tools the application executes the function and returns a tool_result.

S2Which is a server tool?

  • AA shell script that runs on your own laptop and calls a service
  • BA database query that is written in your own application code
  • CA custom get_policy function
  • Dweb_search, which runs on Anthropic's servers
Show the answer

Answer: D. Server tools such as web search and code execution run on Anthropic's infrastructure.

S3A tool call arrives with stop_reason: "tool_use". What must the application do next?

  • AIgnore it
  • BEnd the conversation and show the user the raw tool request
  • CRerun the request without tools to get a plain text answer
  • DRun the tool and return a tool_result with the same tool_use_id
Show the answer

Answer: D. The loop continues by returning the result for the specific call.

S4A tool fails with a timeout. What should the harness return to Claude?

  • AA random value so that the loop keeps going
  • BAn empty success
  • CA tool_result with is_error: true and a clear message
  • DNothing, and crash the whole application
Show the answer

Answer: C. Structured errors let the model recover; crashes and fake successes hide the failure.

S5Claude keeps choosing get_customer when the user asks about a policy, because both descriptions are three words long. What is the best first step?

  • ARewrite descriptions with purpose, inputs, examples and boundaries
  • BMerge all of the tools into one large general tool
  • CSwitch models
  • DAdd a separate routing classifier before every call
Show the answer

Answer: A. Descriptions are the primary selection signal; improve them before adding infrastructure.

S6A tool initiates payments. Which control is most appropriate?

  • AHuman confirmation and code validation, with an idempotency key
  • BLetting the model decide silently whether to pay
  • CRunning it twice for safety, in case the first run fails
  • DA prompt sentence saying "be careful"
Show the answer

Answer: A. Sensitive actions need enforced approval and safe retry behavior.

S7Which TWO describe good tool set design? Select TWO.

  • AMany overlapping tools so the model has choices
  • BReturning only the fields the next step needs
  • CExposing write access to every tool
  • DOne tool that does everything with a free-text mode argument
  • EFew, distinct tools with clear boundary-stating descriptions
Show the answer

Answer: B, E. Distinct, well described tools and concise results improve selection and keep context small.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Definition name, description, input_schema
Round trip tool_use (stop_reason: tool_use) → run → tool_result (same id) → continue until end_turn
Dispatch Harness maps tool name to code; validate input; model arguments are untrusted
Client vs server Client tools run in your app (internal systems); server tools (web_search, web_fetch, code_execution) run on Anthropic's side
Errors tool_result with is_error: true and a useful message; timeouts; idempotency
Approval Auto for read-only; human confirmation or hooks for sensitive actions
Tool set Few, distinct, well described, least privilege, concise results
